natural_body: Deep discounts spike signups +31% but risk renewal. Use tactically with guardrails.

first.rationale: The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and two inherited memories (86: shorter onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value; 31: fewer signup fields lifts SMB first-week activation) speak directly to it. Simplifying onboarding also blunts the competitor's price pressure on price-sensitive SMBs by improving perceived time-to-value rather than by cutting price, which protects sustainable qualified revenue. I am deliberately verifying the two memories my choice actually rests on rather than the ones I am rejecting: memory_86 and memory_31 are the load-bearing claims, and if their source records show weak effect sizes, short measurement windows, or that the lift was measured only on activation proxies without any renewal follow-through, the case for this slot collapses and activation_messaging (memory_91) becomes the better in-product lever. Rejected promotional_pricing despite memory_73's +31% signup spike: that memory itself carries an explicit renewal-risk caveat, and a signup spike against a price-led competitor is exactly the case where short-term volume is most likely to be non-durable revenue. Rejected referral_incentive (memory_57) and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) as off-target for the observed SMB/self-serve decline. Downstream value risk: cutting signup fields can degrade lead qualification data and admit lower-intent accounts, so the experiment must be read on qualified-account and week-four retention outcomes, not raw completion. Uncertainty preserved: all six memories are consolidated summaries, some 40-60 days stale, and none were formed under current competitive pricing conditions; the archived records may not reproduce their headline claims, so I commit to a standard experiment with a holdout rather than a broad rollout.
